notes: Labels in this file describe what a careful HUMAN would decide for each
item, given the raw comparable-listing data provided -- NOT what the
current app/comparable_search.py + app/pricing.py code actually
produces. Several cases are deliberately designed to document known
weaknesses in the current implementation (brand-only fallback noise,
defekt/Bastler/Ersatzteile majorities, 'Suche ...' wanted ads and
placeholder EUR1 prices polluting the median, and the all-new-condition
fallback overpricing used goods) and are EXPECTED to fail today -- see
backend/tests/test_eval_accuracy.py, which ratchets on the
currently-measured baseline rather than requiring 100%.
price_type ambiguity note (see bead sandbox-8jm.1 AMBIGUITY section):
kleinanzeigen-api 0.4.0 WAS installed and inspected directly (not
assumed). Listing.price_type is copied RAW from the live API's
'price-type' field (kleinanzeigen_api/client.py:472) -- i.e. listings
returned by search() carry the API's own internal values, not the
library's easy-to-type create-ad input aliases. client.py's
_PRICE_TYPE_MAP (client.py:1215-1219) shows the mapping from those
input aliases to the actual API values: 'FIXED' -> 'SPECIFIED_AMOUNT',
'NEGOTIABLE'/'VB' -> 'PLEASE_CONTACT', 'FREE'/'GIVE_AWAY' -> 'FREE'.
cli.py:240-241 confirms the same three real values are what search
filtering matches against ('SPECIFIED_AMOUNT', 'PLEASE_CONTACT',
'FREE'). So the three price_type strings used in this fixture data are
'SPECIFIED_AMOUNT', 'PLEASE_CONTACT', and 'FREE' (the actual value used
for 'Zu verschenken' listings) -- 'FIXED', 'NEGOTIABLE', and
'GIVE_AWAY' are only create-ad input aliases and never appear on a
real Listing. current app code ignores price_type entirely (see
comparable_search.py's _listing_to_raw), so this is included in the
raw dicts for future-proofing only and has no effect on today's
decisions.

cases.description: Straightforward working item with several closely-clustered comparable prices; the joined query matches on the first attempt. Documents the happy path -- code and human should agree.
Working but low-value item; comparables cluster well below EUR10, so the human agrees the item should be given away rather than sold.

Item is broken/unusable. Even though comparable *working* units sell for real money, a careful human would not try to sell or give away a broken TV -- throw_away wins regardless of comparables. price_type/price data is irrelevant here so expected_price_range is null.

Obscure item; every candidate query (there is only one, since the joined query equals the single keyword) returns a valid, empty result set. Label follows the documented rule in app/pricing.py's module docstring (point 2): 'no comparables found at all -> throw_away', a deliberate design choice (no market signal at all to act on) rather than a bug -- so throw_away is the correct expected label here, not a documented weakness.

Joined query 'bosch akkuschrauber' returns zero results. The loosening logic's next candidate would normally be the brand-only keyword 'bosch', but bead sandbox-8jm.5 skips that candidate entirely (a lone brand name as a fallback query mostly surfaces unrelated same-brand products, e.g. the dishwasher/mixer/iron below), and instead falls back to the next, genuinely relevant keyword 'akkuschrauber'. Before sandbox-8jm.5, the code would have queried 'bosch' and priced the item off those unrelated listings (median ~45 EUR); after sandbox-8jm.5 it prices off the relevant used-drill listings instead (~EUR20) -- code and a careful human should now agree.

Joined query 'bosch akkuschrauber' returns zero results. The brand-only keyword 'bosch' is skipped by sandbox-8jm.5's relevance gate, and the remaining fallback keyword 'werkzeug bosch' returns other Bosch-branded tools whose titles share no token with the identified name 'Bosch Akkuschrauber' (no 'akkuschrauber' overlap) -- e.g. a jigsaw and an angle grinder, not a cordless screwdriver. With no relevant comparables found at all, the documented pricing rule (app/pricing.py docstring point 2: no comparables -> throw_away) applies -- code and a careful human should agree there's no market signal to price off here.

Joined query 'nike laufschuhe gr 42' returns zero results, so the loosening logic falls back to the individual keyword 'laufschuhe', which returns genuinely relevant running-shoe listings. This is the loosening mechanism working as intended -- code and human should agree.

The item itself works fine (condition good), but the comparable-listing search happens to surface mostly 'defekt/Bastler/Ersatzteile' (broken/for-tinkerers/spare-parts) listings at very low prices, plus one genuinely working comparable at a normal price. KNOWN WEAKNESS: code has no filter for defekt/Bastler/Ersatzteile listings (that's bead sandbox-8jm.4) so the low-priced junk listings dominate the median and drag the decision down to give_away; a careful human would recognize those as not-comparable and price off the one working listing instead -- expected to FAIL both decision_correct and price_in_range today.

All comparables are genuine 'Zu verschenken' (give-away) listings at EUR0, with price_type set to the give-away value ('FREE' -- see top-level notes). Both code and human agree: this item is only worth giving away, so expected_price_range is null (a concrete price isn't meaningful for a free item).

The search surfaces several 'Suche ...' (wanted/looking-to-buy) ads posted at a nominal EUR1, mixed with a couple of genuine sale listings. KNOWN WEAKNESS: code doesn't distinguish demand ('Suche') ads from supply (sale) ads, so the EUR1 wanted-ad prices dominate the median and the decision drops to give_away; a careful human would exclude the wanted ads and price off the two real sale listings -- expected to FAIL both decision_correct and price_in_range today.

Several genuine sale listings (not 'Suche' wanted ads) use EUR1 as a placeholder/negotiable-price marker rather than a real asking price, mixed with a couple of listings with real prices. KNOWN WEAKNESS: code takes every listed price at face value, so the EUR1 placeholders dominate the median and the decision drops to give_away; a careful human recognizes EUR1 + 'VB' as a placeholder and prices off the real listings instead -- expected to FAIL both decision_correct and price_in_range today.

Every comparable listing is condition 'Neu' (brand new/retail). Code's new-condition filter would normally exclude 'Neu' listings, but since that would leave zero comparables it falls back to the full unfiltered (new-priced) list -- overpricing a used item. KNOWN WEAKNESS: decision (sell) still happens to match, but the suggested price (~95 EUR, retail-level) is well above what a careful human would price a used version at (~55 EUR, applying a typical used-goods discount) -- expected to FAIL price_in_range today.

Only one comparable listing was found. NOTE: the label below (sell, ~EUR40) is a defensible human call given the single relevant, on-topic match, but the real issue this case documents is confidence, not correctness -- a decision built on exactly one data point should ideally be flagged as low-confidence rather than treated the same as a decision backed by many listings. A later bead (decision_confidence) is expected to address this; until then this case just pins today's (reasonable) point-estimate behavior.

All comparables are condition 'wie neu' (like new / excellent used condition) -- a distinct, common tier from 'Neu' (brand new) that must NOT be excluded by the new-condition filter. Code and human should agree here: this documents correct current behavior.

cases.description: Item condition is 'unknown' (identification wasn't sure what the item even is, not that it's broken). Code treats unknown as usable/not-broken and proceeds normally; a careful human, seeing a physically-present item with decent comparables, agrees. Documents correct current behavior.

bead sandbox-0as: working item whose comparable listings mention broken-listing terms only in negated form ('nicht defekt', 'kein Bastlerartikel', 'defektfrei') -- these are genuine working comparables and must stay in the median, alongside one genuinely broken 'defekt' listing that must still be dropped. Documents the negation-aware _filter_broken_listing_titles fix (no exclude= forwarded to the provider any more).

bead sandbox-182: joined query 'makita akkuschrauber makita akku schrauber' and the individual keyword 'makita akkuschrauber' both return zero results, so the loosening logic reaches keyword 'akku schrauber' (the brand-only keyword 'makita' is skipped per sandbox-8jm.5). All 4 results genuinely refer to the item but are spelled differently from the identified_name 'Makita Akkuschrauber' -- hyphenated ('Akku-Schrauber') or space-split ('Akku Schrauber') compound spellings. Before sandbox-182, the plain casefolded-substring relevance gate required the literal one-word substring 'akkuschrauber' and rejected all 4 (no listing spelled it as one word), leaving zero comparables and (incorrectly) a throw_away decision; after sandbox-182, the compacted-title match (all non-alphanumeric characters stripped before comparing) accepts all 4 -- code and a careful human should now agree.

bead sandbox-182: multi-word brand 'Black & Decker'. The joined query returns zero results. The loosening logic's next candidate would be the differently-punctuated brand-only keyword 'Black+Decker' -- an exact-string brand comparison (pre-sandbox-182) would NOT recognize this as brand-only (it doesn't equal 'Black & Decker' as a whole string), so old code queries it, and old code's relevance gate has the same whole-string bug (it never recognizes 'black'/'decker' as brand tokens either), so it wrongly treats the unrelated Black & Decker appliance results below as 'relevant' (their titles contain the words 'Black'/'Decker') and stops there -- pricing the item off junk appliances and reaching the wrong decision. sandbox-182's per-token brand comparison correctly recognizes 'Black+Decker' as brand-only (both its folded tokens, 'black' and 'decker', are brand tokens) and skips it, falling through to the generic keyword 'akkuschrauber', which returns genuinely relevant cordless-screwdriver listings -- code and a careful human should now agree.
